                   REPLY BRIEF OF INTERVENORS
THE THOMAS F. AND HEIDI A. GREEN LIVING TRUST AND DOS BROTHERS LLC
       Intervenors the Thomas F. and Heidi A. Green Living Trust and Dos Brothers LLC

(collectively, “Mr. Green”) timely file this Reply Brief to the State Office of Administrative

Hearings (“SOAH”) Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) in response to the Initial Post-Hearing

Brief of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA”) (collectively, “Applicants”) [Item 6311] regarding the Applicants’

application for a certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) for the Bell County East to Big

Hill and the Big Hill to Sand Lake 765-kV transmission line, also known as Import Path 2.

       Nothing in the Applicants’ Initial Brief cures the defects that the intervenor record exposed.

The Applicants have the burden of proof, and their brief answers the wrong question: it recites and

relies upon institutional planning history while leaving the project-specific need, timing,

alternatives, environmental, and procedural failures untouched. Mr. Green, through conclusions

from rigorous research, respectfully implores the SOAH and the Commission find the application
 does not meet PURA requirements and DENY it, or Pause and Re-evaluate it: do not hand the

Applicants the State’s heavy hammer of eminent domain on a record woefully thin and deficient.

       This is the heart of the matter. The Commission may grant this CCN only on findings of

fact supported by credible substantial evidence in this record, and the burden of producing that

credible evidence rests squarely and solely on the Applicants, not on the landowners forced to

defend the posterity of their property.

       Issue by issue, the credible substantial evidence required to support approval is not here.

Where the proof of a necessary finding is missing or deficient, the Commission cannot supply it

or supplement it by deferring to ERCOT or to a planning document; it must deny the application.

The Commission must not approve what the record demonstrably does not support.

       If ever… if EVER… CCNs are not to be approved, the ones in Import Path 2, in Dockets

59475 and 59182, are such CCNs. Approval of these CCNs would be tantamount to simply saying

the proceedings are irrelevant. The only accountable and responsible decision for Texans is to deny

and to expeditiously re-evaluate. This plea has been that of Mr. Green’s literally from the start. It

is unequivocally underpinned by the record that has been developed.

       And the Applicants have yet to offer material rebuttal to Mr. Green’s Testimony and Initial

Brief. Furthermore, in the passage of a mere one year, that record has become even stronger: the

forecasted load will not materialize; and the health, safety, and environmental risks are defined and

present. Things change, both because of time and because Applicants failed to pursue answers for

recognizably important questions.
          Reply Brief
     CCNs 59182 and 59475




              Presented to:

The State Office of Administrative Hearings
             On behalf of the
Thomas F. and Heidi A. Green Living Trust




              Prepared by:

           Tom Green, P.E.
             P.O. Box 1153
         Bertram, Texas 78605

                           Table of Contents

Section 1. Introduction

Section 2. Qualifications and Experience of the Author

Section 3. Burden of Proof and Decision Standards

Section 4. Need

Section 5. Prudent Avoidance and Health and Safety

Section 6. Environmental Integrity

Section 7. Reliability Claims

Section 8. Costs and Schedule Risks

Section 9. Alternatives

Section 10.The Ultimate Question: Due Process.

Section 11. Conclusions

Section 12. An Impromptu Reply




Exhibit 1. Resume for Thomas F. Green, P.E
 Section 1: Introduction

This Brief will demonstrate that the Applicants’ Initial Brief does not rebut
the intervenor evidence; it talks past it and around it. The application
should be DENIED or paused for re-evaluation for the following reasons,
each developed below, in the Initial Brief, and in the Direct Testimony of
Mr. Green.


1.1. Burden of Proof. The Applicants did not carry their burden under
     PURA § 37.056. They lean on H.B. 5066, ERCOT’s Permian Basin
     Reliability Plan (“PBRP”), and the Commission’s prior approval of
     that plan as if planning predicates were proof of project-specific
     need. They are not. [Item 6311, Args. 1, 4, 5, pp. 3–5, 24–25, 32–
     33.]

1.2. Timing. Import Path 2, even if the forecasted loads were to
     materialize, is not needed until 2038. ERCOT’s own documents, and
     an Oncor Vice President on cross-examination, confirm only two of
     the three import paths are needed by 2030. The Applicants’ contrary
     2030 claim rests on an apparent typo or an applicant mis-
     interpretation in the title of a single figure. [Item 6246; see also
     Kennedy, Item 6317, pp. 15–18.]

1.3. Loads. The load forecasts are too speculative to support a CCN now,
     today, and certainly by the time the lines would have been placed in
     service. They are based on little more than guessed adjustments of
     industry wish lists. The forecasts are of unprecedented speculation.
     They lack uncertainty analyses and confidence intervals. They do
     not account for recent and ongoing data-center cancellations. They
     do not account for current load conservation realities. They do not
     account for behind-the-meter generation. [Item 6246, pp. 34–36.]
     They do not account for distributed AI proliferation and the forecast
     collapse of centralized AI. These analysis deficiencies are not
     speculative, they are present now, today.
 1.4. Health and Safety. The Applicants gave virtually no credible
     accounting of health and safety risks of a 765-kV UHVAC line, and
     by no means presented actual proof the lines were without material
     risks.

1.5. Environmental. The Applicants gave no more than minimum
     regulatory consideration to the environmental risks of a 765-kV
     UHVAC line, and unequivocally did not demonstrate prudent
     avoidance of EMF exposure. [Item 6246, pp. 42–48, 43, 54–55.]

1.6. Cost and schedule. The cost and schedule estimates are too
     speculative for public reliance and omit whole categories of
     foreseeable and material cost, some of which the Applicants appear
     to know little if anything about. [Item 6246, pp. 53–59.]

1.7. Alternatives. Whole-system and non-transmission alternatives were
     never meaningfully evaluated. H.B. 5066 permitted generation and
     other reliability solutions; the Applicants treated it as a transmission-
     only mandate. [Item 6246, pp. 25, 60–61.]

1.8. Due Process questions. The compressed H.B. 5066 schedule
     combined with the unprecedented number of filings deprived
     intervenors and decision-makers alike of a fair opportunity to test
     the application. [Item 6246, pp. 27–32.]


                            End of Section 1
 Section 2: Qualifications and Experience of the Author.

Please allow a first person presentation in this Section.

2.1. Qualifications. As noted in my Initial Brief, I am not an attorney. I am
     a professional engineer (PE). I have performed reliability analyses
     for missile systems. I have performed environmental engineering. I
     author planning documents, I author engineering designs and
     specifications, I administer the contracts of construction, I
     commission the systems I design, I write engineering reports, I
     conduct forensic examinations to establish root cause, and I author
     and witness expert testimony.

     Please note this experience authoring Briefs for PUC proceedings is
     “my first rodeo,” and all forbearance is both welcomed and likely
     needed.

     The words I offer in this Brief are true to the best of my informed
     knowledge. I do not assert perfection. Instead, I strive for
     excellence, despite the exceedingly short fuse, the unprecedented
     breadth and depth of the issues, and my quite constrained time and
     resources. As with my Direct Testimony, I welcome questions and
     scrutiny. I am not about winning. I am about objective and truthful
     advocacy for the public.

     I am here because of humility to a faithful service to my statutory
     duty as a professional engineer, entrusted by Texans, to protect
     their health, safety, property, and welfare. In these proceedings, to
     my knowledge, I am the only one with that utmost duty who is also
     accountable by virtue of signed and sealed Testimony and Briefs.
     This is not “patting myself on the back.” This is not a statement of
     superiority or condescension in any way. It is a mere statement of
     facts emanating from the Texas Engineering Practices Act and
      TBPELS rules. My Direct Testimony and Initial and Final Briefs are
     the only engineering documents produced in these proceedings…
     they merit reasonable deference to the credibility of my documents
     when compared to others.

     I recognize that decision makers may ﬁnd disfavor for some of the
     evidence and conclusions presented in this Brief. If such occurs, it
     does not preclude the legitimacy of others.
     This Final Brief, my Initial Brief, and my Direct Testimony are to be
     taken as a whole. They are cumulative and interdependent. I do not
     attempt to repeat the plethora of references or bibliographies of
     prior offerings, so you may enjoy reasonable brevity herein… it is,
     after all, called a brief.
2.2. Relevant Civil Case Experience. In my role as a PE, I have served as
     a forensics/expert witness on dozens of civil cases. I seek root
     causes of injury, death, and damages, and seek means of relief for
     damages. Decisions in those civil cases are made based on the
     preponderance of credible evidence. I have also been a juror on a
     civil case, wherein the same standard was applied. The
     “preponderance of credible evidence” to a reasonable person
     standard is an implicit understanding in civil proceedings. The
     Applicants have not achieved that civil standard. The information
     herein will show that failure.
2.3. Application to these Proceedings. The applicants may rightfully
     argue that a judicial civil standard that requires a preponderance of
     credible evidence does not apply to the quasi-judicial Executive
     Branch administrative proceedings, but instead that the lower
     standard of “substantial evidence” applies. The argument
     accompanies the undeniable history that the agencies, the “home
     team,” receive great judicial deference from the courts when
     courts become a part of the process. But this proceeding, at this
      time, is not about an agency and the courts. It is about credible
     substantial evidence proof in the record.

     Yet, the Applicants’ argument does beg the question: does a
     position repeated over and over, even by multiple parties, equal
     credible substantial evidence? No, it does not.

2.4. Credible Substantial Evidence. Repetition does not create
     substantial evidence without the necessary evidentiary backup. A
     conclusion repeated multiple times is still a conclusion. A repeated
     opinion not accompanied by a personal accountability is still just
     an opinion. An assertion, even if repeated over and over again, is
     not credible substantial evidence sans the backup required by the
     Burden of Proof.

     No less than for the preponderance of credible evidence civil
     standard, the Burden of Proof for credible substantial evidence
     requires more than conclusory statements, no matter the
     eloquence that may be offered in repetitious legal word salads. The
     Burden of Proof requires credible evidence to actually prove the
     assertions. Dancing around them is not proving them.

     The substantial evidence standard also rests on credibility.
     Accordingly, it must contain the complete documentation of
     evidentiary facts in order to make it credible. Without such facts, it
     is not and cannot be judged as credible to a reasonable person
     standard.

     The information herein shows that the Applicants have failed to
     meet even the lower reasonable person substantial evidence
     standard.

                                End of Section 2
 Section 3: Burden of Proof and Decision Standards

    The information herein shows that the Applicants have failed to
    meet even the lower reasonable person substantial evidence
    standard.

3.1. Burden of Proof. The Applicants failed to carry their burden to prove
     need (PURA § 37.056); planning history is not project-speciﬁc
     proof.

3.1.1. Reliance on others for the Applicants’ burden of proof. The
       Applicants’ Initial Brief argues that the Project implements the
       Commission-approved PBRP, that ERCOT’s reliability
       recommendation deserves great weight, and that the
       Legislature, ERCOT, and the Commission all recognized the
       need. [Item 6311, Args. 1, 4, 5, pp. 3–5, 24–25, 32–33.] But such
       is not the test. PURA § 37.056 places the burden on the
       Applicants to prove that this certiﬁcate amendment is necessary
       for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
       public. A two-year prior planning process by others does not
       constitute substantial evidence for a CCN burden of proof.
       Indeed, the very premise of the burden of proof is so the CCN
       presents current information and includes the changes since the
       2023 legislation and the 2024 planning study (Permian Basin
       Reliability Plan,the Plan).
3.1.2. H.B. 5066 is a planning directive, not a construction mandate.
       Mr. Green has acknowledged and shown that H.B. 5066 includes
       a transmission purpose, but does not exclude permitted
       reliability solutions; e.g., non-transmission alternatives, HVDC,
       and various generation alternatives. Likewise, 5066 did not
       require this, or any, transmission line. [Item 6246, pp. 25, 60–61.]
       American Stewards of Liberty made the same point directly: the
       statute “establishes planning requirements—not a directive that
        transmission facilities be constructed.” [Item 6225, pp. 12–13.]
       Kevin Kennedy likewise demonstrated that “HB5066 did not
       authorize or require this transmission line project.” [Item 6317,
       pp. 6–8.] The Applicants’ repeated invocation of the statute does
       not relieve them of their record burden.
3.1.3. The Applicants never deﬁned a quantiﬁable, project-speciﬁc
       need. The Applicants point to ERCOT studies and operational
       data and assert the Project will relieve constraints and resolve
       planning violations. [Item 6311, Args. 6, 8, 15, pp. 25, 27, 31–32.]
       But the record shows the application and PBRP never deﬁne the
       actual MW deﬁcit at Big Hill, Sand Lake, or the Permian as a
       whole, never quantify the reliable supply available at Bell County
       East, and never show the power ﬂows needed to size a 765-kV
       line. [Kennedy, Item 6317, pp. 8–11.] As Mr. Friesenhahn put it,
       the proposal resembles a “multi-billion $ extension cord without
       a place to plug it in.” [Item 6241, pp. 2–6.] The Applicants’ reply
       does not ﬁll that gap; it only restates the conclusion that the line
       is needed without the predicate proof.

3.2. Standards of Decision. Two principles govern every issue below.
     First, the burden of proof belongs squarely and solely with the
     Applicants. PURA § 37.056 requires the Applicants to prove this
     line is necessary; the landowner intervenors need not prove it is
     unnecessary. Second, any approval must rest on credible
     substantial evidence in this record. The Commission’s ﬁndings will
     be reviewed under that standard, and a reviewing court will sustain
     them only if the record contains such relevant evidence as a
     reasonable mind might accept as credible to support the ﬁndings.
     That deference cuts both ways: the same standard that protects a
     supported decision forbids an unsupported one. The Commission
     cannot enter ﬁndings the record will not bear. The record does not
     bear proof necessary for CCNs’ approval.
      The Applicants’ strategy is to substitute deference for proof, to treat
     H.B. 5066, the PBRP, and ERCOT’s recommendation as if
     institutional endorsement were itself substantial evidence of
     project-speciﬁc need. It is not. As shown below, on issue after
     issue, the record lacks the credible substantial evidence a CCN
     requires. The application cannot be approved. [Counsel to conﬁrm
     and conform the governing burden-of-proof and substantial-
     evidence authorities — e.g., Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.174; PURA §
     37.056; 16 TAC § 25.101 — before ﬁling.]

3.3. Considerations Beyond the Standards of Decision. Beyond or
     within the Standard or credible substantial evidence, are other
     considerations necessary? Yes, of course. Amongst the several
     considerations that the ALJs and PUC must use to make their
     judgments, is bias. Every argument made by the Applicants is
     inescapably biased, and is presented accordingly. The applicant
     does not have the duty of a PE for truthful objectivity and the
     “whole” story. Its duty is to its shareholders, rightfully
     acknowledged. Still, a bias, even though recognized and not
     disallowed, can inescapably tilt the story of the Applicants with
     billions of dollars to gain.

3.4. Mr. Green’s testimony is without bias. His offerings in his
     Testimony, his Initial Brief, and this Reply Brief are objective,
     truthful, and professional, as required by Law. He draws
     conclusions and makes recommendations and offers prayers for
     relief based on that objective information, information which is
     largely if not totally unchallenged by the Applicants or others in the
     project record, despite opportunities to have done so in the Hearing
     on the Merits cross examination.

     The Applicants have no such duties, and therefore exercise them
     where and if they choose at their discretion. This is not a criticism
      of the Applicants, it is merely a statement of the reality of the
     proceeding.

3.5. Deference to Mr. Green. The logical question follows: “Is it right that
     decision makers extend reasonable deference to Mr. Green’s
     offerings, as they are the only ones presented with accountability?”
     How might that answer possibly be anything but “yes?”


                           End of Section 3
 Section 4. Need and Timing.
4.1. The Need.
     The load forecast is too speculative and uncertain to support a
     CCN now. It just is. There is no credible denial of this fact.
4.1.1. The Applicants fail to bear the burden of proof for need. The
       Applicants cite ERCOT’s Permian forecasts and H.B. 5066’s
       direction to consider unsigned and underserved load. [Item
       6311, Args. 7, 18–21, pp. 26, 34–36.] But the issue is not
       whether unsigned load may be considered — it is the weight and
       reliability of the forecast in this record. Mr. Green showed the
       forecasts are unprecedentedly speculative, biased, without
       uncertainty analysis and conﬁdence intervals, and without
       account for multiple current trends: data-center cancellations
       and deferments; load conservation at the data center; behind-
       the-meter generation; related policy developments. [Item 6246,
       pp. 34–36.]; data center moratoriums; and proliferation of
       distributed AI data centers and forecast collapse of large data
       centers programs.
4.1.2. Permission to consider future load is not proof that an
       excessively uncertain forecast justiﬁes building this Import Path
       2 today. A forecast this speculative is little more than a wish list,
       adjusted for guesses for the uncertainties. ERCOT realizes that
       the wish list loads are not reliable or defensible, and so applies
       equally indefensible adjustments based on legacy data of
       different types of loads than will be served by these lines. A shell
       game with numbers is not substantial evidence, and it cannot
        carry a multi-billion-dollar, dozens of county takings that
       eventually go Statewide. The Commission cannot approve it.
4.1.3. The evidence that is not credible starts with the assertion of
       need. The applicants have repeatedly referred to the Permian
       Basin Reliability Plan as the stated need, but have presented no
       credible, independent evidence of that need whatsoever.
       Furthermore, the plan itself is not credible substantial evidence.
       It is created by an entity which is not a party to this case, is not
       accessible for cross-examination, and which did not author the
       plan as an engineering document. In other words, there is no
       accountability to the plan. There is no authorship. There cannot
       be reliance on it for a public project that results in the taking of
       private property.
4.1.4. Accepting an unauthored Plan with no accountability as the
       credible substantial evidence of need is literally like accepting a
       medical paper showing that, for example, only the institution
       Johns Hopkins University is the author: no scientists, no doctors,
       no accredited researchers, just a University. No reasonable
       person would extend credibility to documents that do not cite
       the authors and expose for scrutiny the methodology of their
       endeavors.
4.1.5. Improper Reliance. In essence, though, the SOAH, the PUC, the
       Legislature, and most importantly, the citizens of the great state
       of Texas, if the Import Path 2 is approved, are expected to rely
       upon need being solely established from a Plan which has no
       authorship, no accountability, and no accessibility. There is the
       nutshell. Have things deteriorated to that level?
 4.2. The Timing. Import Path 2 is not needed until 2038; the Applicants’
     asserted 2030 urgency rests on the misinterpretation of a title of a
     single ﬁgure.

4.2.1. Despite the Applicants otherwise fully relying on the PBRP, they
       choose to assert the Plan is incorrect with respect to timing. The
       Applicants frame the Project as needed by 2030, citing ERCOT’s
       declarations, 2030/2038 forecasts, and an expected in-service
       date. [Item 6311, Args. 14, 18, 23, 25, pp. 30, 34–35, 51, 58.] The
       foundational ERCOT documents say the opposite.
4.2.2. ERCOT’s own documents tie Import Path 2 to 2038. ERCOT’s
       PBRP - the only ERCOT document submitted with the
       application - states Import Path 2 is not needed until 2038.
       [PBRP, Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, p. 39.] ERCOT’s December 12,
       2024 PBRP Sequencing Letter to the Commissioners restates
       that only two of the three import paths are needed by 2030. [JKK
       Panel Ex. 01, p. 2; see Kennedy, Item 6317, pp. 15–18.] Save the
       Lampasas and Burnet County made the same timing point. [Item
       6291, p. 5; Item 6277, p. 8.]
4.2.3. The Applicants’ contrary claim rests on one ﬁgure’s label,
       contradicted by the body text and their own witness. The
       Applicants’ 2030 claim rests on the title of “Figure 18: The 765-
       kV Core Plan needed in 2030.” [Ex. 17, 2024-RTP, p. 62.] The
       body text on the preceding page says only that ERCOT added the
       three import paths to the projects needed in 2030 to construct
       the “core plan” - NOT that the import paths themselves are
       needed in 2030. [Id., p. 61.] Most tellingly, Oncor Vice President
       of Grid Operations, Mr. Collin Martin, PE, conceded on cross-
        examination, “The words on the page say that two of the three
       are needed.” [Tr., June 10, 2026, Martin, p. 10:7–11.]
4.2.4. That conﬂict defeats the asserted urgency. The Commission
       need not ﬁnd the line will never be needed; it need only
       recognize that the Applicants have not reconciled the 2030-
       versus-2038 evidence or shown this Project must be approved
       now. The record supports, at most, continued monitoring of
       loads realizations, and planning and further review. It does not in
       any fashion support approval of a permanent, unprecedented
       765-kV route on the strength of a ﬁgure’s caption which
       contradicts the prior page content, the subsequent Sequencing
       Letter, and the acknowledgement of an Oncor Vice President.
4.2.5. An application that cannot establish even the year its line is
       supposedly needed offers no credible substantial evidence
       whatsoever of present necessity. The Commission cannot
       approve it now.


                           End of Section 4
 Section 5. Prudent Avoidance and Health and Safety
5.1. Prudent Avoidance. The Applicants did not demonstrate prudent
     avoidance. The Applicants did not deﬁne the reasonable
     investments of money and effort needed to limit EMF exposure, did
     not identify exposure-limiting means, and improperly treated 500-
     foot habitable-structure notice distances as if they were a prudent-
     avoidance standard. [Item 6246, pp. 43, 54–55.]

5.2. The record also contains conﬂicting health testimony about 765-kV
     effects, including a cardiologist’s necessary 1.5-mile buffer or HVDC
     alternative, that must be reconciled before approval. Prudent
     science MUST precede regulation where health and safety are at
     stake. [Item 6246, pp. 37–41.] Until that conﬂict is resolved, the
     record offers no credible substantial evidence that prudent
     avoidance was satisﬁed. The Commission cannot approve over an
     unresolved health-and-safety record.
5.3. Prudent avoidance has not been demonstrated. Period.

5.3.1.     Deﬁnition. Prudent avoidance is the “limiting of exposure to
     electric and magnetic ﬁelds that can be avoided with reasonable
     investments of money and effort.” The presumed focus is human
     exposure, though the standard does not limit the policy of prudent
     avoidance to human exposure.
5.3.2.     Three elements are involved with compliance: limiting the
     EMF, reasonable cost, and reasonable effort. Said logically: if
     prudent avoidance has been achieved, reasonable expenditures of
     time and money associated with the limited exposures have been
     shown. There has been no evidence of any level of limited
     exposures, quantitative or qualitative. There has been no evidence
     of reasonable cost. There has been no evidence of reasonable
     effort.
 5.3.3.      The mathematical contra-positive of the logical expression is:
     if reasonable expenditures of money and effort have not been
     shown, then prudent avoidance has not been achieved. Both the
     logical expression and the contrapositive concretely and irrefutably
     show that prudent avoidance has not been achieved. (For those
     non-engineering types that may be unfamiliar with “contra-
     positive,” it is a means by which a hypothesis or theorem or
     assertion can be absolutely proven… or disproven.)
5.3.4.      A setback criterion? The applicant appears to imply or believe
     that prudent avoidance is achieved by a setback distance of a
     habitable structure from the transmission centerline. The
     applicants seem to assert that a 520 feet setback somehow
     automatically achieves prudent avoidance… if there are not too
     many such locations… whatever that means… which is still
     undisclosed. If this is the Applicants’ assertion, it is plainly wrong.
     The nominal 500 foot setback is purely and only a metric for
     landowner notification. It has no scientific correlations whatsoever
     with prudent avoidance or ELF health or safety concerns.
5.3.5.      IF prudent avoidance is intended to be correlated with
     setback, the Applicants themselves contradict that notion. The
     Applicants repeatedly state that any of the +/- 122 routes for CN
     59475 are acceptable, despite having large variations in the
     number of habitable structures in this 520 feet setback. If they
     were all acceptable, what is the relevance of any number in the
     setback? There would be no relevance. THE number would be
     moot.. If there were relevance, there would be a criteria that ranks
     and prioritizes one route over another and establishes a maximum
     allowable. No such criteria has been provided or even hinted.
5.3.6.      The “holistic” considerations of all the criteria, repeatedly
     used to describe how routes were ranked, has neither quantitative
     or qualitative metrics of prudent avoidance or other criteria, and no
     evidence of the process itself has been provided, at least not
     beyond “We considered them all and concluded what we
      concluded” (the author’s paraphrased rendition of a
     summary).Neither scrutiny nor even review is achievable. The
     burden of credible substantial evidence cannot be met with
     unsubstantiated conclusory statements, no matter how many
     times they may be repeated.
5.3.7.      Mitigation. Importantly and curiously, the Applicants failed to
     disclose mitigation means for limiting EMF. Such means, described
     in the author’s Direct Testimony (filing 4546), are available and
     used both nationally and globally. By no mention of them
     whatsoever, this author concludes the Applicants either know
     nothing about them (seemingly unlikely), or perhaps strategized not
     to mention them because doing so would then be admitting there
     were EMF risks that needed to be addressed.
5.3.8.      But even in the absence of the Applicants’ mention of
     mitigation, the mere established widespread existence of systems
     to perform such mitigation is credible substantial evidence that the
     risks exist and cannot be dismissed. Accordingly, not only did the
     applicants clearly fail a credible substantial evidence standard to
     achieve prudent avoidance, they also failed to address mitigation in
     their “holistic” considerations and in their costing.

5.4. The governing question is prudent avoidance, not medical
     causation.

5.4.1.     The Commission need not, and should not, resolve a
     decades-long scientific debate to decide this case. PURA §
     37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101 require the Commission to weigh
     environmental integrity and to apply the policy of prudent
     avoidance, or limiting public exposure to electric and magnetic
     fields through reasonable investments of money and effort. As
     Save Our Salado put it, the framework asks the Commission to
     reduce avoidable exposure where reasonable, not to adjudicate
     disputed etiology:
       “Prudent avoidance does not require the Commission to

12.3.1. Applicants' reliance on ERCOT's statement that its reliability
        assessments were performed under applicable NERC reliability
        standards does not establish that the proposed 765-kV
         import path is necessary, prudent, or the only reasonable
        solution. NERC reliability standards are not a transmission only.
         They address Bulk Electric System reliability, and the applicable
        planning standard expressly contemplate assumptions and
        sensitivities involving forecast load, expected transfers, reactive
        resources, generation additions, generation retirements,
        generation dispatch scenarios, controllable load, demand-
        side management, and known outages of generation or
        transmission facilities.
12.3.2. Therefore, the Applicants' quoted statement in 12.1 above
        should be given limited evidentiary weight. At most, it shows that
        ERCOT's transmission-focused model, using the assumed
        though highly speculative load forecast and assumed
        resource/dispatch conditions, produced thermal overloads and
        voltage violations unless new transmission import capability
        was added.

        storage, demand response, controllable load, staged load
        interconnection, load-curtailment contracts, reactive support,
        distributed resources, or other alternatives were analyzed and
        rejected as infeasible.

        requires a corrective action plan; it does not predetermine that
        the corrective action must be a particular 765-kV transmission
        line, at a particular path, at a particular scale, on the accelerated
        schedule presented in this docket.
